name: Tria Beauty hair removal laser

card.summary: An at-home diode laser for hair reduction, one of two over-the-counter diode devices the FDA had cleared as of 2025.
card.note: Dark, coarse hair on lighter skin responds best; light, grey, red and fine hair respond poorly.

quick.overview:
The Tria is a consumer diode laser for hair removal at home. According to Wikipedia, it is one of two diode devices the US FDA had cleared for over-the-counter sale as of 2025.

Laser hair removal in clinics is described as producing long-term hair reduction rather than total removal, usually needing several sessions. Sources specific to the Tria were limited, so this article is short.
quick.mechanism: Laser energy is absorbed by melanin in the hair and heats the follicle (selective photothermolysis), damaging it while sparing most surrounding skin. Treatments are repeated over weeks to months.
quick.risks: Common effects are redness, itching and swelling lasting a few days; burns, pigment changes and eye injury are possible. Results vary by hair and skin colour.

lead: The Tria is a hair-removal diode laser sold for home use. People use it to reduce unwanted hair on the legs, underarms, bikini line, face and body, aiming for smoother skin and a long-term drop in regrowth without repeated clinic appointments, waxing or daily shaving. Wikipedia states that, as of 2025, the US FDA had cleared two diode devices for over-the-counter sale, the Epilaser and the TRIA.[1]

Professional laser hair removal works by selective photothermolysis: light absorbed by melanin heats the hair follicle.[1] It is cleared for "permanent hair reduction", meaning a long-term decrease in regrowth rather than total removal.[1] Dark, coarse hair on light skin responds best, and most people need at least eight sessions spaced 3 to 8 weeks apart.[1]
infobox: Dark, coarse hair on light skin[1]
At least eight sessions, 3 to 8 weeks apart[1]

paras: Wavelength and pulse duration are chosen so melanin absorbs most of the energy. Dark, coarse hair on light skin responds best; light, red, grey, white and fine hair respond poorly. [1] Most people need at least eight sessions spaced 3 to 8 weeks apart. [1]

Common short-lived effects include itching, redness and swelling for two or three days; acne and skin discoloration are the most serious common effects, with burns and infection also reported. [1] Review literature notes diode lasers had the most side effects in one comparison. [1]

Wikipedia notes that in Florida an over-the-counter device may be used by anyone as long as they do not perform laser hair removal commercially, and that its page carries a note that device clearance information may be dated.[1]
No studies found on the Tria specifically. For the category, a randomized trial cited in encyclopedic sources reported 69.2% hair reduction with a diode laser versus 52.7% with IPL at 12 months.[1]

A 2023 PLoS One study in 15 women compared six underarm treatments with a professional diode laser or a different home-use device (the Silk'n Flash and Go Lux, not the Tria). The professional laser reduced hair by about 85 to 88 percent and the home device by about 46 to 52 percent, with mild side effects and no serious adverse events; the authors concluded the home laser reduced hair at a slower rate and noted eye safety as a concern with long-term home use.[2]

chain: Pulses of diode laser light absorbed by hair melanin
Fewer and finer regrowing hairs over repeated sessions

angle.text: Users treat unwanted hair at home with repeated laser sessions, aiming for a lasting reduction in hair count and smoother skin. Results depend on hair and skin colour, and treatments are repeated over weeks to months.
